Endosperm
• It is a nutritive tissue which provides nourishment to the developing embryo.
• It is a Triploid structure formed by mitotic divisions of primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).
• Depending upon the mode of its formation, Angiospermic endosperm is mainly of three types.
a. Nuclear endosperm b. Cellular endosperm c. Helobial endosperm
a. Nuclear endosperm
• It is the most common type of endosperm found in several angiosperms.

• In this type, PEN under goes repeated divisions without wall formation producing a large number of
free nuclei.
• A vacuole appears in the Centre and pushes the cytoplasm containing the nuclei to the periphery.

wheat, rice.
• In coconut there is an outer white kernel multicellular solid endosperm and the centre is filled with free

1. Nuclear type: In this type of endosperm, the repeated mitotic division of PEN is not accompanied
by wall formation. The nuclei produced are free in the cytoplasm of the embryo sac. They may
remain free indefinitely or wall formation takes place later.
2. Cellular type: In this case, each division of PEN is followed by cytokinesis, hence forms a
triploid endosperm tissue accompanied by wall formation. The cells of this tissue are filled with
reserve food materials and are used for the nutrition of developing embryo.
3. Helobial type: It is an intermediate type. The first nuclear division is accompanied by cytokinesis
but the subsequent ones are free nuclear.

groundnut.
• In some seeds the developing embryo do not consumes the endosperm completely. Such seeds persist
even at maturity are known as albuminous seeds or endospermic sees. E.g.: - Castor, Coconut, wheat,
maize, barley, sunflower

Structure of Dicot embryo/Stages involved in the development of Dicot embryo
Stages in the development of a Dicot Embryo
• The zygote divides transversely and produces a two celled proembryo of unequal sized cells.
• The larger cell lying towards micropylar end is the basal cell or suspensor cell and the smaller cell
lying towards chalazal end is the terminal cell or embryo cell.
• The suspensor cell undergoes a number of transverse divisions to form a filament of 6 to 10 suspensor cells.
• The first cell of the suspensor lying towards micropylar end becomes swollen to form Haustorium.
• Last cell of the suspensor functions as hypophysis and later gives rise to radicle and root cap.
• The embryo cell undergoes longitudinal divisions twice and at right angles to each other to form 4
cells. These 4 cells then divide to form 8 cells or octet stage.
• Out of these 8 cells the lower 4 cells give rise to plumule and 2 cotyledons while the upper 4 cells
give rise to radicle and hypocotyl.
• All the 8 cells undergo periclinal divisions to form outer single layered epidermal cells called
dermatogen and inner layers of promeristem and procambium.
• Initially the embryo is globular later with the growth of cotyledons it becomes heart shaped and
finally the suspensor cells degenerate and mature embryo is formed.
• This type of dicot embryo development is called as Crucifer type/Onagrad type.
Structure of Dicot embryo
• A typical dicot embryo consists of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons.
• The portion of embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the
epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule (stem tip).
• The cylindrical portion below the level of cotyledons is the hypocotyl that
terminates at its lower end in the radicle (root tip).
• The root tip is covered with a root cap.
Structure of Dicot seed
• All dicotyledonous seed consists of the following parts.
a. Seed coat: It consists of two layers namely, an outer thick layer called testa which is impermeable
to water. The inner thin layer called tegmen which is permeable to water.
b. Embryo: In dicot seed the embryo consists of the following parts.
i. Embryonal axis:
• It is made up of meristematic tissue (promeristem) which gives rise to epicotyls and hypocotyl.
• Epicotyl gives rise to plumule, which develops into shoot system and hypocotyl gives rise to
radicle which develops into root system.
ii. Embryonal axis: It is a specialized structure of embryonal axis where two cotyledons are attached.
iii. Cotyledon: There are two cotyledons and they provide nutrition for developing embryo.

Structure of Monocot seed
All monocotyledonous seeds consist of the following parts
a. Embryonal axis:
• It is made up of meristematic tissue gives rise to plumule and radicle.

Seed
• A seed is defined as fertilized ovule formed inside the fruit.
• A typical seed consists of seed coat and an embryo.

• The two integuments of the ovule become the seed coat. The outer integument forms testa while the
inner integument develops into tegmen.
• The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat and it facilitates the entry of oxygen and water
into the seed during germination.
• Within the seed coat there is an embryo. It consists of embryonal axis to which one or two cotyledons
are attached. The embryo may enter into a state of inactivity called Dormancy.
• The embryo is surrounded by a nutritive tissue called endosperm.
• Depending upon on the presence and absence of endosperm the seeds classified into two types.
They are
1. Seeds which retain some amount of endosperm even at maturity as it is not completely used up
by the developing embryo are called endospermic seeds or albuminous seeds.
E.g.: - Maize, Sunflower, Castor, barley, wheat
2. Seeds which do not retain and have no residual endosperm at maturity as it is completely
consumed by the developing embryo are called non-endospermic seeds or ex-albuminous seeds.
E.g.: - Pea, Bean, Groundnut.
• Occasionally in some seeds like black pepper, beet and coffee, remnants of nucellus is also persistent.
This residual persistent nucellus or the degenerated part of nucellus of ovule is called perisperm.
NOTE
• In a few species the seeds loose viability (able to germinate) within a few months.
• Seeds of a large number of species live for several years. Some seeds can remain alive for hundred
years.
• There are several records of very old yet viable seeds.
• The oldest is that of a Lupine, Lupinus arcticus excavated from Arctic Tundra. The seed germinated
and flowered after an estimated record of 10,000 years of dormancy.
• A recent record of 2,000 years old viable seed is of the Date palm, Phoenix dactylifera discovered
during the archaeological excavation at King Herod’s palace near Dead Sea.
Importance of Seeds
1. Dependable method: Pollination and fertilization of seed plants are independent of water. These two
reproductive processes are free from requirement of water, hence seed formation is more dependable.
2. Perennation: Seed is dry with dormant embryo and thick protective seed coat. It is most suitable for
perennation through unfavourable periods.
3. Dispersal: Seeds have better adaptive strategies to get dispersed to new habitat and help the species to
colonise in other areas.
4. Reserve food: Seeds have sufficient quantity of reserve food for nourishing the young seedlings.
5. Protection: Hard seed coat provides protection to young embryo.
6. Variations: As they are formed due to sexual reproduction, they produce plants with new variations
and better genetic recombination. Variations are essential for adaptability to diverse environmental
conditions.
7. Agriculture: Seed is the basis of agriculture. They can be used as food throughout the year and also
to raise crop in the next season.

Apomixis
• The phenomenon of formation of seeds without fertilization is called Apomixis.
E. g: - Asteraceae and grasses.
• It is a type of asexual reproduction where new individuals are formed without the formation and fusion
of gametes.
• Thus, apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.
• It is found in some angiosperms particularly in Grasses.
• The term apomixis was coined by Winkler in 1908.
• The seeds formed by apomixis are called Apomitic seeds.
• There are several ways of development of apomitic seeds.
E. g: - In citrus and mango embryos are formed directly from a diploid cell outside the embryo sac
either the nucellus or the integument.
Significance/advantages of Apomixis
• Production of hybrid seeds is costly and too expensive to the farmers.
• The hybrids plants produce from such seeds do not retain the character but the character segregate in
them.
• Hybrid varieties of several crops are being extensively cultivated because of their increased productivity.
Polyembryony
• The phenomenon of having more than one embryo in a seed or occurrence of more than one embryo in
a seed is called Polyembryony.
E. g: - Orange, Mango, Onion
• More often, as in many Citrus and Mango varieties some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo
sac dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into the embryos. In such species each ovule
contains many embryos.

HUMAN REPRODUCTION
SEXUAL DIMOPHISM IN HUMAN BEINGS
• Human beings, like most of mammals, are unisexual or dioecious (sexes are separate) sexually
reproducing and viviparous.
• Each human being has only either male or female gonads, reproductive ducts and accessory genital
structures.
• Out of these reproductive structures, gonads (testes in male and ovaries in females) are called primary
sex organs and produce the gametes and sex hormones.
• All other genital structures (reproductive ducts and associated glands) are collectively called
secondary sex organs. These include epididymis, vas deferens, prostate gland, seminal vesicles and
penis in male, and the Fallopian tubes (oviducts), uterus, vagina and mammary glands in females.
• Two sexes are also different in their certain external morphological features, called secondary or
accessory sexual characters, while this phenomenon is called sexual dimorphism.
• Sexual dimorphism can be studied by two types of sexual characters.
• After the child birth, primary sexual characters are mainly used to detect sex of a child. In males,
primary sexual characters are a pair of testicles and a penis. In female, primary sexual characters are
vaginal apparatus pair of ovaries and uterus.
• Once an individual reaches adolescence starts exhibiting secondary sexual characters.

(i) Formation of spermatids: - It takes place in 3 phases

consists of cytoplasm sheath and axial filament. End piece consists of only axial filament.

of sperm”.

• Axial filament (Axoneme) is a thin, long, thread like structure derived from distal centriole. It runs
throughout the length of tail. It helps in the locomotion of the sperm.

• It is a regular and cyclic process in which some complex process occurs in the female reproductive

• During this phase the empty graafian follicle forms corpus luteum.
• Corpus luteum secretes a hormone called progesterone.
• Progesterone brings about further thickening of endometrium and inhabits the production FSH and
LH from pituitary gland.
• If the fertilization does not take place corpus luteum degenerates into corpus albicans.

• The cells of embryonic disc exhibit continuous mitotic division and produce new cells.
• These new cells spread between embryonic disc and endoderm. These cells represent mesoderm and

on land either inside egg or in the uterus of mother. These are not formed in anamniotes as their

removal of wastes.
• Amnion is the innermost embryonic membrane and never participates in placenta formation.
• Chorion is the outermost embryonic membrane and always participates in placenta formation.
Types of placenta
(i) On the basis of foetal membranes involved in the formation of placenta
Placentae are of 3 types
(a) Yolk sac placenta – Formed of Yolk sac and chorion. e.g., marsupials like kangaroo, opossum.
(b) Allantoic placenta – Formed of allantois and chorion. e.g., most of eutherians
(c) Chorionic placenta – Formed of only chorion. e.g., primates
(ii) On the basis of intimacy between foetal and maternal blood, placenta is of 5 types on the basis
of number of layers separating their bloods
(a) Epitheliochorial – 6 layers – e.g., odd hoofed mammals (horse, pig)
(b) Syndesmochorial – 5 layers – e.g., Even – hoofed mammals (Cow, sheep, goat, camel etc.)
(c) Endothelialchorial – 4 layers - e.g., Carnivores (Dog, cat, lion, tiger etc.)
(d) Haemochorial – 3 foetal layers – e.g., Primates (Monkey, apes, lemurs, human female)
(e) Haemoendothelial – only foetal blood capillary – e.g., rodents and lagomorphs (rabbit)
PREGNANCY/GESTATION
• The period taken by the embryo for its development is called pregnancy or parturition. Gestation
period in humans lasts for 9 months (280 days).
ORGANOGENESIS
• The process of formation of organs and organ system during early development is called
organogenesis.
• After one month of pregnancy heart is formed and starts functioning.
• In First month, there is formation of blood vessels and neural tube. The formation of heart is the first
sign of growth.
• Limbs and digits are formed at the end of second month of foetus.
• In the second month primitive characters such as tail and pharyngeal gill slits are also formed.
• At the end of first trimester or third month (12th week) all primitive characters disappear and
external genitalia is developed. (Sex of the foetus can be determined in the third month).
• In the Fourth month all organ systems develop and the developing foetus will have human
appearance.

Biology Human Reproduction
47 Department of Biology
• At the end of Fifth month first movement of foetus takes place.
• At the end of Sixth month or Second trimester (24th weeks) body is covered by tiny hair (Lanugo),
eye lids separate and eye lashes are formed.
• On the Seventh month complete development of foetus takes place and on the Eighth month if the
foetus is male testicles enters into scrotum.
• At the end of ninth month the fully developed foetus exerts pressure of uterine wall which lead to
parturition.
PARTURITION
• Expelling of fully formed young ones from the mother’s uterus through vaginal orifice after gestation
period is called parturition or it is the process of giving birth to a baby.
• In human being, gestation period is about 280 days/9.5 months from the start of the mother’s last
menstruation.
• Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism.
• The fully developed foetus and placenta induces mild contraction of uterus. It is called foetal ejection
reflex.
• During parturition, foetus secretes hormones from its adrenal gland. These hormones diffuse into
mother blood and reaches posterior part of the pituitary gland to produce a special hormone called
oxytocin (birth hormone).
• Oxytocin stimulates uterine endometrium which helps in uterine contraction. At the same time,
oxytocin stimulates placenta to produce prostaglandin chemicals, and these chemicals stimulates
uterine wall and also internal orifice of the cervix for the easy parturition of baby.
• During parturition time, labour pain develops i.e. forceful contraction of uterine wall leads to more
pain during parturition is called labour pain.
• As the birth approaches, the foetus fully positioned in such a way that head is facing towards cervix.
• Parturition can be studied under three stages
(a) Dilation stage: -
• It takes about 12 hours; during this stage regular peristaltic contraction of uterine wall begins
from its top and moves downwards. As the result, foetus moves downwards to the cervix.
• Here amnion and chorion ruptures, amniotic fluid passes out leads to lubrication of vaginal
orifice.
• Now foetal placenta pulled out from the uterine wall and foetus becomes free from maternal
tissues.
(b) Expulsion: -
• It takes about 20 minutes.
• Here contraction of uterine wall is more powerful followed by abdominal wall contraction as
a result baby’s head comes out of the cervix.
• Here, umbilical cord is cut near the baby; this frees the baby totally from mother.
• Now relaxin hormone induces relaxation of pelvic girdle ligament which leads to easy birth.
(c) After-birth
• It takes about 12 minutes.
• After baby’s birth, uterus become relaxed as a result, placenta becomes free from the
implantation site.

Biology Human Reproduction
48 Department of Biology
• Now placenta, umbilical cord, foetal membrane ruptured, blood capillaries and same amount
of blood expelled out due to series of rhythmic contraction and relaxation of myometrium part
of uterus. Now, immediately after birth cervix released to prevent excess bleeding.
• After 25-30 days, uterus returns fully to its non-pregnancy state.
LACTATION
• Synthesis, secretion and ejection of milk in female after child birth are called lactation or production
of milk in mammary glands during pregnancy and after pregnancy is called lactation.
• The milk that is produced for 2 or 3 days after parturition is yellowish in colour and contains large
number of antibodies (IgA) is called colostrum or first milk.
• The antibodies present in colostrum provide innate immunity to the newly born baby.
• Mechanism of lactation can be studied under 2 phases
(a) Milk secretion
• Milk production takes place after the formation of placenta under the influence of prolactin
hormone.
• But maximum milk secretion takes place after the child birth because the sucking of the nipple
around the areola part stimulates receptors of hypothalamus PRF- Prolactin releasing factor.
(b) Milk ejection
• It involves ejection of milk from mammary glands and laticiferous ampulla by oxytocin.
COMPOSTION OF MILK
• Milk produced after few days of child birth which is slightly yellowish in colour with excess
antibodies is called Colostrum.
• It consists mainly the antibody IgA
• Milk consists of Na, K, Ca, P, lacto albumin, casein protein, lipid, lactose sugar, various types of
antibodies and excess water.
NOTE
• Progesterone is called pregnancy hormone and Oxytocin is called birth hormone or labor
hormone.
• Oxytocin is usually injected to the pregnant woman at the time of parturition to facilitate contraction
of uterine wall.

CHAPTER – 1
SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS
Characteristics of Angiosperms
• They are commonly called flowering plants or phanerogams.
• They are commonly known as closed seed plants, because the ovules are covered by ovary.
• They are the most advanced group of plants both physiologically and anatomically.
• They are most advanced tracheophytes (both xylem and phloem are well developed).
• The members exhibit double fertilization.
• The endosperms are always triploid in nature.
Flower
• Flower is a highly condensed reproductive shoot of a
plant or it is a special reproductive branch meant for
sexual reproduction.
• The study of flower is called Anthology.
Parts of a flower
• Pedicel – It is the stalk of the flower.
• Thalamus/Receptacle – It is the tip of the pedicel becomes flattened or disc like holds or supports all
the floral parts. Thalamus bears four floral parts. They are
a) Calyx
• It is the outermost floral part and green in colour.
• It helps in photosynthesis and gives protection when flowers are in bud condition.
• The individual units of calyx are called sepals.
b) Corolla
• It is the second floral whorls brightly coloured due to the presence of a pigment called
Anthocyanin.
• It helps in attraction of birds and insects for pollination.
• The individual units of corolla are called petals.
c) Androecium
• It is the third floral whorl and called male reproductive part.
• The individual units are called stamens.
• Each stamen consists of anther, connective and filament.
d) Gynoecium
• It is the inner most floral whorl and called female reproductive part.
• The individual units are called pistil or carpel.
• Each pistil consists of ovary, style and stigma.

2 Department of Biology
Note
• Both calyx and corolla are called Accessory whorls because they do not take part in sexual reproduction.
• Both Androecium and gynoecium are called essential or necessary whorls because they directly and
actively take part in sexual reproduction.
Note: Perianth: a flower in which calyx and corolla are undifferentiated and is called perianth. Such a
flower is called homochlamydous flower. A unit or segment of perianth is called tepal. Eg: flower of
champaka coconut , onion etc
Functions of flower
• It helps in production of pollen and ovules.
• It aids in pollination.
• It provide nectar to attract certain pollinator
• It helps in fertilization. After fertilization ovary is the one which develops into a fruit
• It helps the ovules to develop into seeds
Steps involved in Sexual Reproduction in flowering plants
1. Pre – fertilization events
2. Pollination
3. Double fertilization
4. Post – fertilization events

b. Development and formation of female gametophyte (embryo)
a. Development and formation of male gametophyte (Pollen grain)
(Stamen, Microsporangium and Pollen grain)
• A stamen is a male reproductive part or unit of a flower or
Microsporophyll of a flower.
• It is made up of 2 parts. Namely anther and filament.
• The filament is a long slender stalk. Its proximal end is attached
to the thalamus or petal of the flower.
• The anther is generally bilobed structure with each lobe having
two theca i.e., they are dithecous.
• It has four-sided structure consisting of four microsporangia.
• The microsporangia develop further and become pollen sacs and
are packed with pollen grains.
NOTE: A dithecous anther is tetrasporangiate, while monothecous
stamen is bisporangiate.
Structure of Microsporangium

Biology Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
3 Department of Biology
• The microsporangium consists of following parts.
a. Anther wall layers b. Connective c. Pollen grain
b. Anther wall layers
• They are derived from primary parietal cell by repeated anticlinal and periclinal division.
• There are four anther wall layers. They are,
1. Epidermis
• It is the outermost anther wall layer.
• It is a single layered made up of compactly arranged rectangular shaped thick-walled cells and
gives protection.
2. Endothecium
• It is the second anther wall layer. It is also a single layered made up of compactly arranged cells.
• At the time of maturity, the endothecial cells produce fibrous thickenings made up of cellulose and
callose.
• These fibrous thickenings are hygroscopic in nature i.e., they absorb moisture content and helps in
dehiscence of anther.
• Some of the endothecial cells are modified into delicate cells called stomium where anther bursts.
3. Middle layer
• It is the third anther wall layer.
• It is made up of 2 to 3 layers of rectangular shaped compactly arranged parenchymatous cells.
• This layer stores reserve food materials and are short lived (ephemeral).
4. Tapetum
• It is the innermost layer of anther wall layer made up of a single layered elongated cell.
• This layer is also called nutritive layer because it provides nourishment to the developing pollen
grains.
• The cells of the tapetum contain dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.
• A group of compactly arranged sporogenous cells are present in the young anther is called
sporogenous tissue.
b. Connective
• At the junction between the two anther lobes specialized conducting tissues are present and are
called connective.
• They provide nourishment to middle layer.
c. Pollen grain
• It is the male gametophyte derived from primary sporogenous cell by meiotic division.
Functions of Tapetum
• It is a chief nutritive layer for developing pollen grains.
• It induces meiotic stimulus to sporogenous cells.
• It produces a highly resistant biological chemical called Sporopollenin, which is responsible for
formation of exine.
• It also produces pollen kit (It is a lipid molecule protects the pollen grain from dehydration).
• It also produces specialized nutritive bodies called Ubisch bodies.

•
• Additional Points for Competitive Examination
•
Tapetum is of two types:
i) Secretory or glandular tapetum: These cells secrete sporopollenin, pollenkitt and
compatibility proteins. These cells provide Ubisch bodies which help in the ornamentation
of exine as they have a chemical called sporopollenin which is deposited on them.
ii) Amoeboid tapetum: Cells undergo breakdown and their entire protoplast move towards
centre to nourish microspores.
Microsporogenesis
• The process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) through meiosis or the
process of formation of microspores or pollen grains from diploid primary sporogenous cell is
called microsporogenesis.
• The primary sporogenous cell undergoes repeated meiotic division to form number of sporogenous
cell.
• Each sporogenous cell gets meiotic stimulus to form microspore mother cell (MMC).
• Each diploid microspore mother cell undergoes meiotic divisions to form four microspores or
pollen grains.
Structure of a mature Pollen grain
• The male gametophyte in angiosperm is called pollen grain.
• It is haploid in nature, spherical in shape and measuring 25 to 50 microns in diameter.
• It is covered by two layers. Namely Exine and Intine.
• Exine is the outer layer made up of highly resistant chemical called Sporopollenin.
• It can withstand high temperature, strong acids and alkalis. There is no known enzyme which can
digest sporopollenin.
• Exine layer is discontinuous which leads to the formation of small aperture called pollen pore or germ
pore through which pollen tube germinate.
• The inner layer is called intine which is thin and made up of cellulose and pectin (pectocellulose).
• The cytoplasm of pollen grain is surrounded by a plasma membrane.
• When the pollen grain is mature it contains two unequal sized cells, namely the bigger vegetative cell
(tube cell) and smaller generative cell.
• Vegetative cell remains in the center and has reserve food materials and large irregularly shaped
nucleus.
• The generative cell is spindle shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus present at the periphery.
• In over 60% of angiosperms, pollen grains shed at 2 cell stage.
• In over 40% of angiosperms, the generative cell divides by mitosis to form 2 male gametes and shed
at 3 cell stage.
• During germination, the intine grows out as pollen tube through one of the germ pores in the exine.

NOTE
• Pollen grains of many species cause severe allergies and bronchial afflictions in some people often
leading to chronic respiratory disorders like asthma, bronchitis etc.
• It may be mentioned that Parthenium or carrot grass that came into India as a contaminant with
imported wheat, has become ubiquitous in occurrence and causes pollen allergy.
• Even the large number pollen grains can be preserved for many years in liquid nitrogen at -1960C.
Such stored pollen grains can be used as pollen banks in crop breeding programmes.
• In some cereals such as Rice and Wheat pollen grains lose viability within 30 minutes of their release.
• In some members of Solanaceae, Rosaceae and Leguminosae the viability of pollen grains maintains
for one month.
Economic Importance of Pollen grain
• Pollen grains are rich in nutrients.
• In recent years it has become a fashion to use pollen tablets as food supplement.
• In Western countries, a large number of pollen products in the form of tablets and syrups are available
in the market.

Female gametophyte/Embryo sac
• In a majority of flowering plants, one of the megaspores is functional while the other three degenerate.
• Only one functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
• The method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed as monosporic development.
• The haploid nucleus of functional megaspore divides mitotically thrice to from 8 nuclei.
• Out of these 8 nuclei. 4 nuclei migrate towards one pole of the embryo sac and the remaining 4 nuclei
migrate towards opposite pole of the embryo sac.
• One nucleus from each pole migrates to the centre of the embryo sac and is called polar nuclei. These
fuse to form secondary nucleus i.e. a diploid secondary nucleus.
• The 3 nuclei at the base of the embryo sac to form the antipodal cells and the other 3 haploid nuclei at
the apex of embryo sac forms the egg apparatus consisting of a central egg cell and 2 lateral
synergids.
• Thus, a typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity has seven cells with eight nuclei.
• The synergid cell wall forms a highly thickened structure called the Filiform apparatus, which play
an important role in guiding the pollen tube to penetrate into the synergid.

Kinds of Pollination
Pollination is of two types. Namely
1.Self-pollination/autogamy
2. Cross pollination/Allogamy.
1. Self-pollination/Autogamy
• The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of the same flower is called self-pollination.
• It takes place in only in those plants bearing bisexual flowers.
• It is of two types. Namely,
a. Homogamy: - In this case both anthers and stigma of a bisexual flower mature at the same time.
E.g.: - Wheat, Rice, Potato.
b. Cleistogamy: - In this case the bisexual flowers never open but always remain closed so that self-
pollination can take place. E.g.: - Ground nut, Pea, Balsam, Commelina.
2. Cross pollination/Allogamy
• The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of another flower is called cross pollination.
• It occurs in all unisexual flowers and in some bisexual flower.
• It is of two types. Namely,
a. Geitonogamy: - In this case cross pollination takes place between two flowers of the same species
born on the same plant. E.g.: - Maize,

• It is functionally cross pollination and requires pollinating agent but genetically they are similar
to autogamy since the pollen grains come from the same plant.
b. Xenogamy: - In this case cross pollination takes place between two flowers of the same species
born on different plants.
Significance of xenogamy
• It brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma, thus induces genetic variation.
• Example: Papaya plants exhibit xenogamy because, unisexual flowers borne on two different plants.
Agents of Cross Pollination
• Since the pollen grains are non-motile the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the
stigma of another flower requires the assistance of external agents.
• These agents are classified into two main categories. Abiotic and Biotic agents.
• The abiotic agents include non-lining agents like wind, water.
• The biotic agents include living organisms such as bats, birds, snails, slugs.
Abiotic agents of cross pollination
1. Anemophily: - The pollination that occurs through the agency of wind. Such flowers are called
anemophilous flowers. E.g.: - Grasses, Maize, Sugarcane etc.
Factors influencing anemophilous pollination
• The flowers are small, inconspicuous, and colourless.
• They do not produce scent and any nectar.
• The stamens have long filaments so that the anthers are freely exposed to wind.
• The pollen grains are small in size, very light, smooth, dry and powdery, so that they can easily
carried by wind.
• Pollen grains are produced in large quantities so that at least some of them reach the flowers.
E.g.: - a) Cannabis produces 5, 00,000 pollen grains.
b) Tassel of maize give rise to 20-25 million pollen.
• Stigma is large, often lobed and feathery, so that the pollen grains in air can be trapped easily.
• Flowers often have a single ovule in each ovary and numerous flowers packed into an
inflorescence.
2. Hydrophily: - The pollination that occurs through the agency of water. Such flowers are called
hydrophilous flowers. E.g.: -Hydrilla, Vallisneria, Zostera.
Factors influencing hydrophilous pollination
• Flowers are small, inconspicuous, and colourless.
• They do not produce scent and nectar.
• Quite rare in flowering plants
• Regular among the lower plant groups such as algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes.
• Calyx, corolla and other floral parts are unwettable.
• Pollen grains are small, non-sticky and coated by wax.
• Stigma is long unwettable and sticky.

• It is a cross fertilization done by plant breeders.
• It is one of the approaches of crop improvement programmes.
• It is a process of crossing of two plants with different characters to produce commercially a superior

• After fertilization certain changes are observed in the flower.
• These changes include endosperm formation, embryo formation, seed formation and fruit formation.

Endosperm
• It is a nutritive tissue which provides nourishment to the developing embryo.
• It is a Triploid structure formed by mitotic divisions of primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).
• Depending upon the mode of its formation, Angiospermic endosperm is mainly of three types.
a. Nuclear endosperm b. Cellular endosperm c. Helobial endosperm
a. Nuclear endosperm
• It is the most common type of endosperm found in several angiosperms.

• In this type, PEN under goes repeated divisions without wall formation producing a large number of
free nuclei.
• A vacuole appears in the Centre and pushes the cytoplasm containing the nuclei to the periphery.
• Later wall formation takes place around the nuclei to form multicellular endosperm. E.g.: - Maize,
wheat, rice.
• In coconut there is an outer white kernel multicellular solid endosperm and the centre is filled with free

1. Nuclear type: In this type of endosperm, the repeated mitotic division of PEN is not accompanied
by wall formation. The nuclei produced are free in the cytoplasm of the embryo sac. They may
remain free indefinitely or wall formation takes place later.
2. Cellular type: In this case, each division of PEN is followed by cytokinesis, hence forms a
triploid endosperm tissue accompanied by wall formation. The cells of this tissue are filled with
reserve food materials and are used for the nutrition of developing embryo.
3. Helobial type: It is an intermediate type. The first nuclear division is accompanied by cytokinesis
but the subsequent ones are free nuclear.

endosperm are known as non-endospermic seeds or ex-aluminous seeds. E.g.: - Pea, bean,
groundnut.
• In some seeds the developing embryo do not consumes the endosperm completely. Such seeds persist
even at maturity are known as albuminous seeds or endospermic sees. E.g.: - Castor, Coconut, wheat,
maize, barley, sunflower
Embryo
• After fertilization, the fertilized egg or zygote develops into an embryo.
• The process of development of mature embryo from diploid zygote is called embryogenesis.
• In the early stages of development, the embryo of dicots and monocots are similar, but in later stages
they differ considerably.
• The development of embryo is endospermic i.e. towards inside.

Structure of Dicot embryo/Stages involved in the development of Dicot embryo
Stages in the development of a Dicot Embryo
• The zygote divides transversely and produces a two celled proembryo of unequal sized cells.
• The larger cell lying towards micropylar end is the basal cell or suspensor cell and the smaller cell
lying towards chalazal end is the terminal cell or embryo cell.
• The suspensor cell undergoes a number of transverse divisions to form a filament of 6 to 10 suspensor cells.
• The first cell of the suspensor lying towards micropylar end becomes swollen to form Haustorium.
• Last cell of the suspensor functions as hypophysis and later gives rise to radicle and root cap.
• The embryo cell undergoes longitudinal divisions twice and at right angles to each other to form 4
cells. These 4 cells then divide to form 8 cells or octet stage.
• Out of these 8 cells the lower 4 cells give rise to plumule and 2 cotyledons while the upper 4 cells
give rise to radicle and hypocotyl.
• All the 8 cells undergo periclinal divisions to form outer single layered epidermal cells called
dermatogen and inner layers of promeristem and procambium.
• Initially the embryo is globular later with the growth of cotyledons it becomes heart shaped and
finally the suspensor cells degenerate and mature embryo is formed.
• This type of dicot embryo development is called as Crucifer type/Onagrad type.
Structure of Dicot embryo
• A typical dicot embryo consists of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons.
• The portion of embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the
epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule (stem tip).
• The cylindrical portion below the level of cotyledons is the hypocotyl that
terminates at its lower end in the radicle (root tip).
• The root tip is covered with a root cap.
Structure of Dicot seed
• All dicotyledonous seed consists of the following parts.
a. Seed coat: It consists of two layers namely, an outer thick layer called testa which is impermeable
to water. The inner thin layer called tegmen which is permeable to water.
b. Embryo: In dicot seed the embryo consists of the following parts.
i. Embryonal axis:
• It is made up of meristematic tissue (promeristem) which gives rise to epicotyls and hypocotyl.
• Epicotyl gives rise to plumule, which develops into shoot system and hypocotyl gives rise to
radicle which develops into root system.
ii. Embryonal axis: It is a specialized structure of embryonal axis where two cotyledons are attached.
iii. Cotyledon: There are two cotyledons and they provide nutrition for developing embryo.

Structure and development of Monocot embryo
• The development of monocot embryo is almost similar to that of dicot
embryo and is referred to as Sagittaria type.
• Here zygote divides transversely producing a two celled proembryo with a
basal cell and a terminal cell.
• The basal cell enlarges to form vesicular suspensor cell and the terminal cell
gives rise to the whole of the embryo.
• The monocot embryo consists of embryonal axis which is attached laterally
to a single shield shaped cotyledon called scutellum.
• The portion of the embryonal axis above the level of attachment of scutellum
is called epicotyl and the portion below the level of cotyledon is called
hypocotyl.
• Epicotyl has the plumule (shoot apex) covered by a sheath called coleoptile.
• The hypocotyl has the radicle and root cap enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath called coleorhizae.

Seed
• A seed is defined as fertilized ovule formed inside the fruit.
• A typical seed consists of seed coat and an embryo.

• The two integuments of the ovule become the seed coat. The outer integument forms testa while the
inner integument develops into tegmen.
• The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat and it facilitates the entry of oxygen and water
into the seed during germination.
• Within the seed coat there is an embryo. It consists of embryonal axis to which one or two cotyledons
are attached. The embryo may enter into a state of inactivity called Dormancy.
• The embryo is surrounded by a nutritive tissue called endosperm.
• Depending upon on the presence and absence of endosperm the seeds classified into two types.
They are
1. Seeds which retain some amount of endosperm even at maturity as it is not completely used up
by the developing embryo are called endospermic seeds or albuminous seeds.
E.g.: - Maize, Sunflower, Castor, barley, wheat
2. Seeds which do not retain and have no residual endosperm at maturity as it is completely
consumed by the developing embryo are called non-endospermic seeds or ex-albuminous seeds.
E.g.: - Pea, Bean, Groundnut.
• Occasionally in some seeds like black pepper, beet and coffee, remnants of nucellus is also persistent.
This residual persistent nucellus or the degenerated part of nucellus of ovule is called perisperm.
NOTE
• In a few species the seeds loose viability (able to germinate) within a few months.
• Seeds of a large number of species live for several years. Some seeds can remain alive for hundred
years.
• There are several records of very old yet viable seeds.
• The oldest is that of a Lupine, Lupinus arcticus excavated from Arctic Tundra. The seed germinated
and flowered after an estimated record of 10,000 years of dormancy.
• A recent record of 2,000 years old viable seed is of the Date palm, Phoenix dactylifera discovered
during the archaeological excavation at King Herod’s palace near Dead Sea.
Importance of Seeds
1. Dependable method: Pollination and fertilization of seed plants are independent of water. These two
reproductive processes are free from requirement of water, hence seed formation is more dependable.
2. Perennation: Seed is dry with dormant embryo and thick protective seed coat. It is most suitable for
perennation through unfavourable periods.
3. Dispersal: Seeds have better adaptive strategies to get dispersed to new habitat and help the species to
colonise in other areas.
4. Reserve food: Seeds have sufficient quantity of reserve food for nourishing the young seedlings.
5. Protection: Hard seed coat provides protection to young embryo.
6. Variations: As they are formed due to sexual reproduction, they produce plants with new variations
and better genetic recombination. Variations are essential for adaptability to diverse environmental
conditions.
7. Agriculture: Seed is the basis of agriculture. They can be used as food throughout the year and also
to raise crop in the next season.

Apomixis
• The phenomenon of formation of seeds without fertilization is called Apomixis.
E. g: - Asteraceae and grasses.
• It is a type of asexual reproduction where new individuals are formed without the formation and fusion
of gametes.
• Thus, apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.
• It is found in some angiosperms particularly in Grasses.
• The term apomixis was coined by Winkler in 1908.
• The seeds formed by apomixis are called Apomitic seeds.
• There are several ways of development of apomitic seeds.
E. g: - In citrus and mango embryos are formed directly from a diploid cell outside the embryo sac
either the nucellus or the integument.
Significance/advantages of Apomixis
• Production of hybrid seeds is costly and too expensive to the farmers.
• The hybrids plants produce from such seeds do not retain the character but the character segregate in
them.
• Hybrid varieties of several crops are being extensively cultivated because of their increased productivity.
Polyembryony
• The phenomenon of having more than one embryo in a seed or occurrence of more than one embryo in
a seed is called Polyembryony.
E. g: - Orange, Mango, Onion
• More often, as in many Citrus and Mango varieties some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo
sac dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into the embryos. In such species each ovule
contains many embryos.

HUMAN REPRODUCTION
SEXUAL DIMOPHISM IN HUMAN BEINGS
• Human beings, like most of mammals, are unisexual or dioecious (sexes are separate) sexually
reproducing and viviparous.
• Each human being has only either male or female gonads, reproductive ducts and accessory genital
structures.
• Out of these reproductive structures, gonads (testes in male and ovaries in females) are called primary
sex organs and produce the gametes and sex hormones.
• All other genital structures (reproductive ducts and associated glands) are collectively called
secondary sex organs. These include epididymis, vas deferens, prostate gland, seminal vesicles and
penis in male, and the Fallopian tubes (oviducts), uterus, vagina and mammary glands in females.
• Two sexes are also different in their certain external morphological features, called secondary or
accessory sexual characters, while this phenomenon is called sexual dimorphism.
• Sexual dimorphism can be studied by two types of sexual characters.
• After the child birth, primary sexual characters are mainly used to detect sex of a child. In males,
primary sexual characters are a pair of testicles and a penis. In female, primary sexual characters are
vaginal apparatus pair of ovaries and uterus.
• Once an individual reaches adolescence starts exhibiting secondary sexual characters.

(i) Formation of spermatids: - It takes place in 3 phases

and non-motile male gametes called spermatids.

it supplies energy for the movement of sperm and hence middle piece is considered as “Engine room
of sperm”.

throughout the length of tail. It helps in the locomotion of the sperm.

• This single layer hollow structure formed from morula is called Blastocyst (Blastula).

• On 7th day the blastocyst attaches to the wall of uterine cavity (endometrium). This process is called

endometrium is called decidua.
• After implantation the decidua present above the blastocyst is called decidua capsularis.
• The decidua present below the blastocyst is called decidua basalis.
• The decidua present opposite to implantation is called decidua parietlis.
Formation of three germ layers
• After implantation, the inner mass cells of the blastocyst undergo repeated divisions and reorganized
into three principle layers called ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
• After implantation the cells found towards the periphery of embryo blast (inner cell mass) of the
blastocyst become flat.
• These flat cells spread along with trophoblast and covers the blastocoel.
• These flat cells represent the endoderm; the cells of embryoblast elongate and become columnar. These
elongated cells represent embryonic disc.
• The cells of embryonic disc exhibit continuous mitotic division and produce new cells.
• These new cells spread between embryonic disc and endoderm. These cells represent mesoderm and
the embryonic disc is called ectoderm.
• Ectoderm, endoderm and mesoderm are the primary germ layers developed from inner cell mass.
• The trophoblast gives rise to extra embryonic membranes. They are amnion, chorion, allantois and
yolk sac.

Biology Human Reproduction
45 Department of Biology
PLACENTA
• After implantation, the blastocyst forms finger like projections called chorionic villi.
• The chorionic villi and the uterine tissue together form the structural and functional unit between the
developing embryo and maternal body called placenta.
• The placenta is connected to the embryo with umbilical cord which helps in the transport of substances
to and fro the embryo.
• Placenta also acts as endocrine gland and produce hormone called HCG [Human Chorionic
Gonadotropin], hPL [Human Placenta Lactogen], estrogen, progesterone and relaxin.
FUNCTIONS OF PLACENTA
• It helps in transportation of nutrients such as glucose and amino acids present in maternal blood into
foetal blood by diffusion.
• It helps in exchange of oxygen and carbon di oxide between maternal blood and foetal blood by
respiration.
• It helps in the excretion of nitrogenous wastes produced in foetus enters into maternal blood through
placenta.
• Placenta is involved in storing of glycogen and iron. It performs the functions of liver.
• Placenta allows the antibodies present in maternal blood to enter into foetus which provide innate
immunity to the newly born baby.
• Placenta acts as impermeable and do not allow the hormones in maternal blood to enter into foetus.
• Placenta is involved in the production of four types hormones and acts as endocrine glands.
• Human chorionic gonadotrophic hormone (hCG): - It maintains corpus luteum to maintain
continuous production of progesterone.
• Human placental Lactogen (hPL) - It activates prolactin which stimulates mammary glands to
produce milk.
• Progesterone: - Placenta after three months starts producing progesterone to maintain pregnancy.
• Relaxin: - It brings about dilation of cervix and helps in parturition.
• Placenta fails to prevent the movement of pathogen into foetus.
• Placenta also fails to prevent the movement of drugs taken during pregnancy into foetus from maternal
blood. These drugs affect the development of foetus.

Biology Human Reproduction
46 Department of Biology
Additional points for Competitive Examination
• Placenta in which there is intimate contact between foetal tissue and maternal tissue is called
deciduate placenta. In such condition during parturition maternal tissue is damaged and leads
to bleeding.
• Placenta fails to prevent the movement of drugs from maternal blood into foetal blood taken
during pregnancy. These drugs affect the development of foetus.
• Thalidomide is a sedative and pain killer given at the time of labour. This drug causes abnormal
development of limbs (seal like limbs) in newly born baby. This condition is called Phocomelia.
• Placenta also fails to prevent the movement of pathogens from maternal blood into foetal blood
if mother is infected at the time of pregnancy.
• Presence of HCG in urine confirms pregnancy. This test is called gravidex test.
• Amnion, chorion and allantois are formed only in amniote embryo as their development occurs
on land either inside egg or in the uterus of mother. These are not formed in anamniotes as their
development occurs in water so there is no problem of desiccation, supply of oxygen and
removal of wastes.
• Amnion is the innermost embryonic membrane and never participates in placenta formation.
• Chorion is the outermost embryonic membrane and always participates in placenta formation.
Types of placenta
(i) On the basis of foetal membranes involved in the formation of placenta
Placentae are of 3 types
(a) Yolk sac placenta – Formed of Yolk sac and chorion. e.g., marsupials like kangaroo, opossum.
(b) Allantoic placenta – Formed of allantois and chorion. e.g., most of eutherians
(c) Chorionic placenta – Formed of only chorion. e.g., primates
(ii) On the basis of intimacy between foetal and maternal blood, placenta is of 5 types on the basis
of number of layers separating their bloods
(a) Epitheliochorial – 6 layers – e.g., odd hoofed mammals (horse, pig)
(b) Syndesmochorial – 5 layers – e.g., Even – hoofed mammals (Cow, sheep, goat, camel etc.)
(c) Endothelialchorial – 4 layers - e.g., Carnivores (Dog, cat, lion, tiger etc.)
(d) Haemochorial – 3 foetal layers – e.g., Primates (Monkey, apes, lemurs, human female)
(e) Haemoendothelial – only foetal blood capillary – e.g., rodents and lagomorphs (rabbit)
PREGNANCY/GESTATION
• The period taken by the embryo for its development is called pregnancy or parturition. Gestation
period in humans lasts for 9 months (280 days).
ORGANOGENESIS
• The process of formation of organs and organ system during early development is called
organogenesis.
• After one month of pregnancy heart is formed and starts functioning.
• In First month, there is formation of blood vessels and neural tube. The formation of heart is the first
sign of growth.
• Limbs and digits are formed at the end of second month of foetus.
• In the second month primitive characters such as tail and pharyngeal gill slits are also formed.
• At the end of first trimester or third month (12th week) all primitive characters disappear and
external genitalia is developed. (Sex of the foetus can be determined in the third month).
• In the Fourth month all organ systems develop and the developing foetus will have human
appearance.

Biology Human Reproduction
47 Department of Biology
• At the end of Fifth month first movement of foetus takes place.
• At the end of Sixth month or Second trimester (24th weeks) body is covered by tiny hair (Lanugo),
eye lids separate and eye lashes are formed.
• On the Seventh month complete development of foetus takes place and on the Eighth month if the
foetus is male testicles enters into scrotum.
• At the end of ninth month the fully developed foetus exerts pressure of uterine wall which lead to
parturition.
PARTURITION
• Expelling of fully formed young ones from the mother’s uterus through vaginal orifice after gestation
period is called parturition or it is the process of giving birth to a baby.
• In human being, gestation period is about 280 days/9.5 months from the start of the mother’s last
menstruation.
• Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism.
• The fully developed foetus and placenta induces mild contraction of uterus. It is called foetal ejection
reflex.
• During parturition, foetus secretes hormones from its adrenal gland. These hormones diffuse into
mother blood and reaches posterior part of the pituitary gland to produce a special hormone called
oxytocin (birth hormone).
• Oxytocin stimulates uterine endometrium which helps in uterine contraction. At the same time,
oxytocin stimulates placenta to produce prostaglandin chemicals, and these chemicals stimulates
uterine wall and also internal orifice of the cervix for the easy parturition of baby.
• During parturition time, labour pain develops i.e. forceful contraction of uterine wall leads to more
pain during parturition is called labour pain.
• As the birth approaches, the foetus fully positioned in such a way that head is facing towards cervix.
• Parturition can be studied under three stages
(a) Dilation stage: -
• It takes about 12 hours; during this stage regular peristaltic contraction of uterine wall begins
from its top and moves downwards. As the result, foetus moves downwards to the cervix.
• Here amnion and chorion ruptures, amniotic fluid passes out leads to lubrication of vaginal
orifice.
• Now foetal placenta pulled out from the uterine wall and foetus becomes free from maternal
tissues.
(b) Expulsion: -
• It takes about 20 minutes.
• Here contraction of uterine wall is more powerful followed by abdominal wall contraction as
a result baby’s head comes out of the cervix.
• Here, umbilical cord is cut near the baby; this frees the baby totally from mother.
• Now relaxin hormone induces relaxation of pelvic girdle ligament which leads to easy birth.
(c) After-birth
• It takes about 12 minutes.
• After baby’s birth, uterus become relaxed as a result, placenta becomes free from the
implantation site.

Biology Human Reproduction
48 Department of Biology
• Now placenta, umbilical cord, foetal membrane ruptured, blood capillaries and same amount
of blood expelled out due to series of rhythmic contraction and relaxation of myometrium part
of uterus. Now, immediately after birth cervix released to prevent excess bleeding.
• After 25-30 days, uterus returns fully to its non-pregnancy state.
LACTATION
• Synthesis, secretion and ejection of milk in female after child birth are called lactation or production
of milk in mammary glands during pregnancy and after pregnancy is called lactation.
• The milk that is produced for 2 or 3 days after parturition is yellowish in colour and contains large
number of antibodies (IgA) is called colostrum or first milk.
• The antibodies present in colostrum provide innate immunity to the newly born baby.
• Mechanism of lactation can be studied under 2 phases
(a) Milk secretion
• Milk production takes place after the formation of placenta under the influence of prolactin
hormone.
• But maximum milk secretion takes place after the child birth because the sucking of the nipple
around the areola part stimulates receptors of hypothalamus PRF- Prolactin releasing factor.
(b) Milk ejection
• It involves ejection of milk from mammary glands and laticiferous ampulla by oxytocin.
COMPOSTION OF MILK
• Milk produced after few days of child birth which is slightly yellowish in colour with excess
antibodies is called Colostrum.
• It consists mainly the antibody IgA
• Milk consists of Na, K, Ca, P, lacto albumin, casein protein, lipid, lactose sugar, various types of
antibodies and excess water.
NOTE
• Progesterone is called pregnancy hormone and Oxytocin is called birth hormone or labor
hormone.
• Oxytocin is usually injected to the pregnant woman at the time of parturition to facilitate contraction
of uterine wall.

Biology Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
1 Department of Biology
CHAPTER – 1
SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS
Characteristics of Angiosperms
• They are commonly called flowering plants or phanerogams.
• They are commonly known as closed seed plants, because the ovules are covered by ovary.
• They are the most advanced group of plants both physiologically and anatomically.
• They are most advanced tracheophytes (both xylem and phloem are well developed).
• The members exhibit double fertilization.
• The endosperms are always triploid in nature.
Flower
• Flower is a highly condensed reproductive shoot of a
plant or it is a special reproductive branch meant for
sexual reproduction.
• The study of flower is called Anthology.
Parts of a flower
• Pedicel – It is the stalk of the flower.
• Thalamus/Receptacle – It is the tip of the pedicel becomes flattened or disc like holds or supports all
the floral parts. Thalamus bears four floral parts. They are
a) Calyx
• It is the outermost floral part and green in colour.
• It helps in photosynthesis and gives protection when flowers are in bud condition.
• The individual units of calyx are called sepals.
b) Corolla
• It is the second floral whorls brightly coloured due to the presence of a pigment called
Anthocyanin.
• It helps in attraction of birds and insects for pollination.
• The individual units of corolla are called petals.
c) Androecium
• It is the third floral whorl and called male reproductive part.
• The individual units are called stamens.
• Each stamen consists of anther, connective and filament.
d) Gynoecium
• It is the inner most floral whorl and called female reproductive part.
• The individual units are called pistil or carpel.
• Each pistil consists of ovary, style and stigma.

Biology Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
2 Department of Biology
Note
• Both calyx and corolla are called Accessory whorls because they do not take part in sexual reproduction.
• Both Androecium and gynoecium are called essential or necessary whorls because they directly and
actively take part in sexual reproduction.
Note: Perianth: a flower in which calyx and corolla are undifferentiated and is called perianth. Such a
flower is called homochlamydous flower. A unit or segment of perianth is called tepal. Eg: flower of
champaka coconut , onion etc
Functions of flower
• It helps in production of pollen and ovules.
• It aids in pollination.
• It provide nectar to attract certain pollinator
• It helps in fertilization. After fertilization ovary is the one which develops into a fruit
• It helps the ovules to develop into seeds
Steps involved in Sexual Reproduction in flowering plants
1. Pre – fertilization events
2. Pollination
3. Double fertilization
4. Post – fertilization events
1. Pre – fertilization events
a. Development and formation of male gametophyte (pollen grain)
b. Development and formation of female gametophyte (embryo)
a. Development and formation of male gametophyte (Pollen grain)
(Stamen, Microsporangium and Pollen grain)
• A stamen is a male reproductive part or unit of a flower or
Microsporophyll of a flower.
• It is made up of 2 parts. Namely anther and filament.
• The filament is a long slender stalk. Its proximal end is attached
to the thalamus or petal of the flower.
• The anther is generally bilobed structure with each lobe having
two theca i.e., they are dithecous.
• It has four-sided structure consisting of four microsporangia.
• The microsporangia develop further and become pollen sacs and
are packed with pollen grains.
NOTE: A dithecous anther is tetrasporangiate, while monothecous
stamen is bisporangiate.
Structure of Microsporangium

Biology Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
3 Department of Biology
• The microsporangium consists of following parts.
a. Anther wall layers b. Connective c. Pollen grain
b. Anther wall layers
• They are derived from primary parietal cell by repeated anticlinal and periclinal division.
• There are four anther wall layers. They are,
1. Epidermis
• It is the outermost anther wall layer.
• It is a single layered made up of compactly arranged rectangular shaped thick-walled cells and
gives protection.
2. Endothecium
• It is the second anther wall layer. It is also a single layered made up of compactly arranged cells.
• At the time of maturity, the endothecial cells produce fibrous thickenings made up of cellulose and
callose.
• These fibrous thickenings are hygroscopic in nature i.e., they absorb moisture content and helps in
dehiscence of anther.
• Some of the endothecial cells are modified into delicate cells called stomium where anther bursts.
3. Middle layer
• It is the third anther wall layer.
• It is made up of 2 to 3 layers of rectangular shaped compactly arranged parenchymatous cells.
• This layer stores reserve food materials and are short lived (ephemeral).
4. Tapetum
• It is the innermost layer of anther wall layer made up of a single layered elongated cell.
• This layer is also called nutritive layer because it provides nourishment to the developing pollen
grains.
• The cells of the tapetum contain dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.
• A group of compactly arranged sporogenous cells are present in the young anther is called
sporogenous tissue.
b. Connective
• At the junction between the two anther lobes specialized conducting tissues are present and are
called connective.
• They provide nourishment to middle layer.
c. Pollen grain
• It is the male gametophyte derived from primary sporogenous cell by meiotic division.
Functions of Tapetum
• It is a chief nutritive layer for developing pollen grains.

Microsporogenesis
• The process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) through meiosis or the
process of formation of microspores or pollen grains from diploid primary sporogenous cell is
called microsporogenesis.
• The primary sporogenous cell undergoes repeated meiotic division to form number of sporogenous
cell.
• Each sporogenous cell gets meiotic stimulus to form microspore mother cell (MMC).
• Each diploid microspore mother cell undergoes meiotic divisions to form four microspores or
pollen grains.
Structure of a mature Pollen grain
• The male gametophyte in angiosperm is called pollen grain.
• It is haploid in nature, spherical in shape and measuring 25 to 50 microns in diameter.
• It is covered by two layers. Namely Exine and Intine.
• Exine is the outer layer made up of highly resistant chemical called Sporopollenin.
• It can withstand high temperature, strong acids and alkalis. There is no known enzyme which can
digest sporopollenin.
• Exine layer is discontinuous which leads to the formation of small aperture called pollen pore or germ
pore through which pollen tube germinate.
• The inner layer is called intine which is thin and made up of cellulose and pectin (pectocellulose).
• The cytoplasm of pollen grain is surrounded by a plasma membrane.
• When the pollen grain is mature it contains two unequal sized cells, namely the bigger vegetative cell
(tube cell) and smaller generative cell.
• Vegetative cell remains in the center and has reserve food materials and large irregularly shaped
nucleus.
• The generative cell is spindle shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus present at the periphery.
• In over 60% of angiosperms, pollen grains shed at 2 cell stage.
• In over 40% of angiosperms, the generative cell divides by mitosis to form 2 male gametes and shed
at 3 cell stage.
• During germination, the intine grows out as pollen tube through one of the germ pores in the exine.

THE PISTIL, MEGASPORANGIUM (OVULE) AND EMBRYO SAC
• The gynoecium (Megasporophyll) represents the female reproductive part of the flower.
• The gynoecium may consist of a single pistil (monocarpellary) or may have more than one pistil

• When there is more than one, the pistils may be fused together (syncarpous).
• Each pistil has three parts, the stigma, style and ovary.
• The stigma is the terminal part of the style which is usually sticky and receives pollen grains during

• The style is the elongated slender part beneath the stigma.
• The ovary bulged part of the pistil is the ovary. Inside the ovary is the ovarian cavity (locule).
• The placenta is located inside the ovarian cavity. From the placenta megasporangia arises which is
commonly called ovules.
• The number of ovules in an ovary may be one (wheat, paddy, and mango) to many (papaya, water
melon, orchids).

• It consists of three parts. Namely, Funicle, Ovule body and Embryo sac.

• It is the female gametophyte located in the nucellus.
• An ovule generally has a single embryo sac formed from a megaspore through reduction division.
• A mature embryo sac has seven cells and eight nuclei.

cells are called Egg apparatus and are present towards Micropyle(egg apparatus consists of one
haploid functional egg cell and two haploid non-functional synergid cells) and one central cell
having diploid secondary nucleus.
• The degenerated part of the nucellus in the ovule is called Perisperm or the residual, persistent
nucellus is called Perisperm. E.g.: - black pepper, beet, coffee etc.

• Ovules generally differentiate a single megaspore mother cell (MMC) in the micropylar region of the
nucellus.

• It is a large cell containing dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus.
• The MMC undergoes meiotic division which results in the production of four megaspores.
Female gametophyte/Embryo sac
• In a majority of flowering plants, one of the megaspores is functional while the other three degenerate.
• Only one functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
• The method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed as monosporic development.
• The haploid nucleus of functional megaspore divides mitotically thrice to from 8 nuclei.
• Out of these 8 nuclei. 4 nuclei migrate towards one pole of the embryo sac and the remaining 4 nuclei
migrate towards opposite pole of the embryo sac.
• One nucleus from each pole migrates to the centre of the embryo sac and is called polar nuclei. These
fuse to form secondary nucleus i.e. a diploid secondary nucleus.
• The 3 nuclei at the base of the embryo sac to form the antipodal cells and the other 3 haploid nuclei at
the apex of embryo sac forms the egg apparatus consisting of a central egg cell and 2 lateral
synergids.
• Thus, a typical angiosperm embryo sac at maturity has seven cells with eight nuclei.
• The synergid cell wall forms a highly thickened structure called the Filiform apparatus, which play
an important role in guiding the pollen tube to penetrate into the synergid.

Pollination
• The transfer of pollen grains from the anther on to the stigma is called pollination.
• Pollination in angiosperms generally takes place at 2 celled stage i.e. pollen having vegetative cell
(tube cell) and generative cell.
• If pollination occurs in closed flowers or the flowers which do not open at all is called cleistogamy
and the flowers are called cleistogamous flowers.
• If pollination occurs in opened flowers i.e., the anthers and stigma are exposed, it is called
chasmogamy and the flowers are called chasmogamous flowers. E.g.: -Viola (common pansy),
Oxalis, Commelina

have limited genetic diversity.
Chasmogamous flowers are with exposed anthers and
stigma, hence autogamy to occur requires synchrony in

Kinds of Pollination
Pollination is of two types. Namely
1.Self-pollination/autogamy
2. Cross pollination/Allogamy.
1. Self-pollination/Autogamy
• The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of the same flower is called self-pollination.
• It takes place in only in those plants bearing bisexual flowers.
• It is of two types. Namely,
a. Homogamy: - In this case both anthers and stigma of a bisexual flower mature at the same time.
E.g.: - Wheat, Rice, Potato.
b. Cleistogamy: - In this case the bisexual flowers never open but always remain closed so that self-
pollination can take place. E.g.: - Ground nut, Pea, Balsam, Commelina.
2. Cross pollination/Allogamy
• The transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of another flower is called cross pollination.
• It occurs in all unisexual flowers and in some bisexual flower.
• It is of two types. Namely,
a. Geitonogamy: - In this case cross pollination takes place between two flowers of the same species
born on the same plant. E.g.: - Maize,

• It is functionally cross pollination and requires pollinating agent but genetically they are similar
to autogamy since the pollen grains come from the same plant.
b. Xenogamy: - In this case cross pollination takes place between two flowers of the same species
born on different plants.
Significance of xenogamy
• It brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma, thus induces genetic variation.
• Example: Papaya plants exhibit xenogamy because, unisexual flowers borne on two different plants.
Agents of Cross Pollination
• Since the pollen grains are non-motile the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the
stigma of another flower requires the assistance of external agents.
• These agents are classified into two main categories. Abiotic and Biotic agents.
• The abiotic agents include non-lining agents like wind, water.
• The biotic agents include living organisms such as bats, birds, snails, slugs.
Abiotic agents of cross pollination
1. Anemophily: - The pollination that occurs through the agency of wind. Such flowers are called
anemophilous flowers. E.g.: - Grasses, Maize, Sugarcane etc.
Factors influencing anemophilous pollination
• The flowers are small, inconspicuous, and colourless.
• They do not produce scent and any nectar.
• The stamens have long filaments so that the anthers are freely exposed to wind.
• The pollen grains are small in size, very light, smooth, dry and powdery, so that they can easily
carried by wind.
• Pollen grains are produced in large quantities so that at least some of them reach the flowers.
E.g.: - a) Cannabis produces 5, 00,000 pollen grains.
b) Tassel of maize give rise to 20-25 million pollen.
• Stigma is large, often lobed and feathery, so that the pollen grains in air can be trapped easily.
• Flowers often have a single ovule in each ovary and numerous flowers packed into an
inflorescence.
2. Hydrophily: - The pollination that occurs through the agency of water. Such flowers are called
hydrophilous flowers. E.g.: -Hydrilla, Vallisneria, Zostera.
Factors influencing hydrophilous pollination
• Flowers are small, inconspicuous, and colourless.
• They do not produce scent and nectar.
• Quite rare in flowering plants
• Regular among the lower plant groups such as algae, bryophytes and pteridophytes.
• Calyx, corolla and other floral parts are unwettable.
• Pollen grains are small, non-sticky and coated by wax.
• Stigma is long unwettable and sticky.
Types of Hydrophily: - It is of two types. Namely, a. Epihydrophily b. Hypohydrophily

Out breeding devices/Contrivances for cross pollination
• Majority of angiosperms produce bisexual flowers and such flowers are likely to get self-pollinated.
• Continuous self-pollination results in inbreeding depression (suitable characters decline).
• To avoid self-pollination and to encourage cross pollination the flowering plants have developed many
devices. They are called out breeding devices.
• Some of the out-breeding devices are as follows.
1. Unisexuality/decliny: It is a condition where plants produce only unisexual flowers. This prevents
self-pollination and encourage cross pollination.
E.g.: -
a. Castor and Maize are monoecious where unisexual male and female flowers borne on same plant
prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.
b. In several species like papaya, male and female flowers present on different plants (dioecious).
This condition prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
2. Dichogamy/Heterogamy: It is a situation where in a bisexual flower the male and female sex organs
mature at different time to avoid self-pollination. There are two types of heterogamy. They are
a. Protandry: It is a condition, where in a bisexual flower the anthers mature earlier before the stigma.
Such flowers are called protandrous. E.g.: - Helianthus, Leucas aspera, Cotton, Sunflower
b. Protogyny: It is a condition, where in a bisexual flower stigma mature earlier before anthers. Such
flowers are called protogynous. E.g.: - Mirabilis, Ficus,
3. Self-sterility/ Incompatibility: It is a condition where even if self-pollination occurs; the pollen grains
fail to germinate on the stigma of same flower due to mutual inhibition. In such plants seeds are

Pollen Pistil interaction
• It is one of the important events takes place in flowering plants before fertilization.
• The events from deposition of pollen grains to the stigma until the entry of pollen tube into the ovules
are referred to as pollen-pistil interaction or after pollination chemical reaction or interaction between
pollen grains and pistil of gynoecium within the flower or between the flowers due to some chemicals
present in them is called pollen-pistil interaction.
• Pollination does not guarantee the transfer of the compatible pollen of the same species as the stigma.
Often, pollen of the wrong type, either from other species or from the same plant even if it is self-
incompatible also deposit on the stigma.
• The pistil has the ability to recognize the pollen of its compatible or incompatible type.
• If it is compatible type, the pistil accepts the pollen and promotes post-pollination events that lead to
fertilization.
• If the pollen is incompatible, the pistil rejects the pollen by preventing pollen germination on the
stigma or the growth of pollen tube in the style.
• Acceptance or rejection between pollen grain and the pistil is mediate by the chemical components.
• The pollen grain germinated on the stigma to produce a pollen tube one of the germ pores.
• The contents of the pollen grain move into the pollen tube. Pollen tube grows through the tissues of the
stigma and style and reached the ovary.
• In few plant species, the pollen grains are shed at two celled stage (a vegetative cell and a generative
cell). In such plants, the generative cell divides and forms the two male gametes during the growth of
the pollen tube.
• In other plant species where pollen grains are shed at three celled stages, pollen tube carries the two
male gametes.
• Pollen tube, after reaching the ovary, enters the ovule through micropyle and then enters one of the
synergids through the filiform apparatus. Recent studies have shown that filiform apparatus present at
the micropylar region guides the entry of pollen tube.

Artificial Hybridization
• It is a cross fertilization done by plant breeders.
• It is one of the approaches of crop improvement programmes.
• It is a process of crossing of two plants with different characters to produce commercially a superior
hybrid with desirable characters. It is one of the major approaches in crop improvement.
• In this technique only the desired pollen grains are used for pollination and the stigma is protected to
prevent contamination from unwanted pollen.
• It can be achieved by two processes. Namely, Emasculation and Bagging techniques.
• Emasculation is a process of removing of anthers in bud condition from the bisexual flowers by using
a pair of forceps without affecting female reproductive organs or by immersing the inflorescence in hot
water with 40-45 ° C for about ten minutes. 𝑖𝑠 This plant is used as female parent for artificial
hybridization.
• The emasculated flowers are covered with a bag made up of butter paper or polythene bag having
minute pores for aeration. The process is called bagging.
• When the stigma of emasculated flowers mature, bag is removed and the desired pollen grains from
male plants are dusted on the stigma using brush. The pollinated flowers are rebagged till fruit
develops.
• Emasculation is not required for unisexual flowers. However, flowers are bagged to prevent
contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen or undesired pollination.
Double Fertilization
• The process of fusion of male gamete with the female gamete is
called fertilization or syngamy.
• After pollination, the pollen grains on the stigma begin to
germinate.
• The pollen grains are shed at two celled stage (a vegetative cell and
a generative cell).
• The exine of the pollen grain ruptures and the intine comes out
through the germ pore in the form of a long narrow pollen tube. The
generative cell divides and gives rise to two male gmetes.
• The pollen tube elongates and reaches the ovule through micropyle
(Porogamy). It is the most common method or through chalazal
end (Chalazogamy) or through integuments (Mesogamy).
• Inside the embryo sac the tip of the pollen tube breaks and the two
male gametes are released.
• One male gamete fuse with the egg cell to form diploid zygote. This is known as first fertilization.
• Second male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei or secondary nucleus to form Triploid Primary
Endosperm Nucleus (PEN). As this involves the fusion of three haploid nuclei and it is called Triple
fusioin.
• Since the fertilization occurs twice and process is called Double fertilization.
• This phenomenon was first reported by S.G Nawaschin (1898) in Lilium and Fritillaria species and
later confirmed by Guignard in 1899.
• After fertilization, the zygote develops into embryo and PEN develops into Endosperm.
Significance of double fertilization
• Fertilization restores diploid number of chromosomes in the zygote.
• The diploid zygote develops into an embryo.

• The PEN develops into endosperm to provide nutrition to the developing embryo.
• The ovule develops into seed and the ovary develops into fruit after fertilization.
• It brings about genetic variations in those plants which exhibit cross pollination.
NOTE: Soon after the process of fertilization, the following changes will take place in a flower by which
the flower is replaced by a fruit.
Calyx – generally falls off
Corolla – falls off
Stamens – falls off
Style and Stigma – shrivel and wither away
Integuments of ovule – become seed coats.
Micropyle – remain as pore in the testa
Synergids and Antipodals – degenerate
Nucellus – absorbed or left as perisperm
Zygote – develops into embryo
Primary endosperm nucleus
in central cell – develops into endosperm
Ovule – develops into seed
Ovary – develops into fruits
NOTE
• The entry of pollen tube into the ovule through chalaza is called Chalazogamy.
E.g.: - Casuarina
• The entry of pollen tube into the ovule through integuments is called Mesogamy.
E.g.: - Cucurbita
• The entry of pollen tube into the ovule through micropyle is called Porogamy.
Porogamy Chalazogamy Mesogamy
Post-Fertilization Events
• After fertilization certain changes are observed in the flower.
• These changes include endosperm formation, embryo formation, seed formation and fruit formation.
• All these events are collectively called post-fetilization events.
Endosperm
• It is a nutritive tissue which provides nourishment to the developing embryo.
• It is a Triploid structure formed by mitotic divisions of primary endosperm nucleus (PEN).
• Depending upon the mode of its formation, Angiospermic endosperm is mainly of three types.
a. Nuclear endosperm b. Cellular endosperm c. Helobial endosperm
a. Nuclear endosperm
• It is the most common type of endosperm found in several angiosperms.
